learning: Iteration 6 (0.6 kg) scored 55.45, so lighter mass hurt. This race tests whether heavier mass reverses the trend. If 1.0 kg beats 69.18, the next single test is 1.2 kg; if not, the mass optimum is near 0.8 kg.
notes: Mass test at 1.0 kg on the iteration 3 baseline. The controller is unchanged from iteration 3 so the score is directly comparable with 69.18.
rationale: The Builder's proposal is a single-variable test of mass on the iteration 3 baseline (80 mm row, 12 mm sensors on a 12 mm pitch, 0.12 m track, 0.03 m wheels, 0.12 m body width, 0.18 m body length). The only change is mass from 0.8 kg to 1.0 kg. Race evidence supports testing heavier mass. Iteration 6 (0.6 kg, otherwise identical) scored 55.45, against 69.18 at 0.8 kg. Oval progress fell from 0.229 to 0.148, so lighter is worse. Max error stays at 0.060 to 0.067 m on every track in every run, so the limit is still breached by bend transients. I keep the iteration 3 controller unchanged (kp 0.8, kd 0.15, ki 0, base_speed 1.5, last_direction, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2]). Keeping the controller fixed makes the 1.0 kg result comparable with 69.18. The heavier robot has more yaw inertia, so it should respond more slowly to a bend transient, but the controller has not been shown to need retuning for that. I do not retune kd, because one variable at a time is needed to tell whether mass alone helps. The sensor geometry is unchanged from the Builder's proposal, which is already the best tested. Expected, not measured: max_error near 0.060 m and a score above 69.18. If the score falls with steering_oscillation rising, the next controller step is a kd change, not a geometry change.
